title: Give drink to the thirsty
hook: a cup of cold water given will not lose its reward
tomorrow: a soldier, a freezing stranger, one cloak. what would you cut?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first work of mercy, feed the hungry, and a king who said a plate set out for the least reached him. You fed me.

Late afternoon heat, and a delivery driver is on your porch, shirt soaked through, already turning back to the van. Do you offer water? It's easy to mean to and forget. John's Gospel puts Jesus in that driver's place. He's tired from the road, sitting by a well in Samaria around midday, with nothing to draw with. A woman comes for water, and he speaks first. In the Douay-Rheims: "Give me to drink." She's startled. Jews and Samaritans keep apart, she says, so why is he asking her?
screen: `A DRIVER IN THE HEAT.` → `A TIRED MAN AT A WELL.` → `GIVE ME TO DRINK.`

segments.voice: That's who asks: the same Jesus who, in Matthew 25, is the king saying, "I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink." Thirst comes right after hunger in the king's list, and it asks for less. A meal takes some doing. Water takes a cup. Earlier in Matthew, Jesus makes the gift about as small as a gift gets: whoever gives one of these little ones a cup of cold water, in the name of a disciple, "he shall not lose his reward." Not a well. Not a feast. A cup. Now the turn. At the well, the one who will go on to offer the woman living water begins by asking her for help. He's worn out, and he lets a stranger give to him. Near the end of John, from the cross, he says it again, out loud: "I thirst." So this work of mercy has two sides. It's the glass offered to a driver on a hot afternoon, the bottle handed through a car window, the cup carried to someone too sick to get up. And it's also being willing to be the thirsty one, and say so, and take the cup someone offers you.
screen: `I WAS THIRSTY.` · `A CUP OF COLD WATER.` · `HE LETS A STRANGER GIVE.` · `I THIRST.` · then, large: `A CUP OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water if one is near, and drink it slowly, noticing the cold, the weight, how it feels to have it at all. Then let one person come to mind who'd be glad of a cup from you: a neighbor, a coworker, someone working outside.
Give drink to the thirsty. A work of mercy as small as a cup, and Matthew's Gospel says even that keeps its reward.
screen: `GIVE DRINK TO THE THIRSTY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Pocket this one: a cup of water, cheap and plain, and asked for by Christ himself at a well. See you tomorrow.
